steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on phonetic word embeddings. It should explain why we need embeddings that capture pronunciation rather than meaning, briefly mention the embedding methods we propose, and present our evaluation suite for phonetic embeddings as the main contribution.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Word embeddings and the (semantic) information they usually carry
- Applications that need pronunciation instead
- Phonetic word embeddings and where they are used
- Our four embedding methods
- The evaluation suite and why it is needed
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - main benefit: compress information into fixed-dimensional vectors
  - used as machine-learning features for NLP applications; studying them reveals linguistic insights
  - often trained with distributional semantics methods -> semantic information
  - example: carrot closer to other vegetables than to ocean
- Need for pronunciation information
  - some applications need a different type of information
  - orthography can obscure pronunciation, esp. in English
  - poem generation: ocean rhymes with motion, not with soybean, though spelling of final syllables suggests otherwise (Figure 1)
- Phonetic word embeddings
  - contain phonetic information; recent interest
  - objective: similar pronunciation -> nearby vectors in embedding space
  - tasks that benefited: cognate and loanword detection, named entity recognition, spelling correction, speech recognition
  - fuller list of applications in Section 6.2
- Our methods
  - four: count-based, autoencoder, metric learning, contrastive learning
  - some inspired by previous work
  - we are first to apply them with supervision from articulatory feature vectors (seldom-exploited linguistic knowledge for representation learning)

  - motivation 2: practitioner picking a method: apply embeddings (fast), then train downstream model (compute/time intensive)
  - intrinsic metrics (cheap) could guide selection before downstream training (expensive), if they correlate with extrinsic metrics

  - prior work evaluates acoustic word embeddings; we focus on text, not speech

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Word embeddings are used everywhere in modern NLP. The main benefit of them is that they compress some information into vectors of a fixed dimension. These vectors can be used as features for machine learning in NLP applications, and studying them can also give linguistic insights. Word embeddings are often trained with methods from distributional semantics, so they carry semantic information. For example, the embedding of the word carrot may be more similar to the embeddings of other vegetables than to the embedding of ocean.

But some applications may need a different kind of information to be encoded. The orthography can hide the pronunciation, especially in English. For instance, a poem generation model may need embeddings that show that ocean rhymes with motion and does not rhyme with soybean, even though the spelling of the final syllables of the words suggests something else (see Figure 1).

Embeddings like this are called phonetic word embeddings. They contain phonetic information, and there has been recent interest in them. The goal is that words that are pronounced similarly should be mapped to vectors that are close to each other in the embedding space. Many tasks have benefited from using phonetic word embeddings, such as cognate and loanword detection, named entity recognition, spelling correction and speech recognition. Section 6.2 has a more detailed list of possible applications.

- Our methods
  - four: count-based, autoencoder, metric learning, contrastive learning
  - some inspired by previous work
  - first to apply them with supervision from articulatory feature vectors (seldom-exploited linguistic knowledge for representation learning)
- Evaluation suite (more important)
  - motivation 1: prior work inconsistent in evaluation -> no long-term improvements observed, no fair comparisons
  - motivation 2: practitioner picking a method: apply embeddings (fast), then train downstream model (compute/time intensive); intrinsic metrics (cheap) could guide selection before downstream training (expensive), if they correlate with extrinsic metrics
  - unlike semantic word embeddings: intrinsic and extrinsic metrics generally correlate
  - prior work evaluates acoustic word embeddings; we focus on text, not speech
- Contributions
  - main: the evaluation suite; no equivalent yet in this subfield
  - also: multiple methods + survey of existing phonetic word embeddings

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Word embeddings are used everywhere in modern NLP. The main benefit of them is that they compress some information into vectors of a fixed dimension. These vectors can be used as features for machine learning in NLP applications, and studying them can also give linguistic insights. Word embeddings are often trained with methods from distributional semantics, so they carry semantic information. For example, the embedding of the word carrot may be more similar to the embeddings of other vegetables than to the embedding of ocean.

But some applications may need a different kind of information to be encoded. The orthography can hide the pronunciation, especially in English. For instance, a poem generation model may need embeddings that show that ocean rhymes with motion and does not rhyme with soybean, even though the spelling of the final syllables of the words suggests something else (see Figure 1).

Embeddings like this are called phonetic word embeddings. They contain phonetic information, and there has been recent interest in them. The goal is that words that are pronounced similarly should be mapped to vectors that are close to each other in the embedding space. Many tasks have benefited from using phonetic word embeddings, such as cognate and loanword detection, named entity recognition, spelling correction and speech recognition. Section 6.2 has a more detailed list of possible applications.

We introduce four methods for phonetic word embeddings: count-based, autoencoder, metric learning and contrastive learning. Some of these techniques are inspired by previous work, but we are the first to apply them with supervision from articulatory feature vectors, which are a form of linguistic knowledge that is seldom exploited for representation learning.

More importantly, we introduce an evaluation suite to test how well phonetic embeddings perform. There are two motivations for this. The first is that prior work does not evaluate models consistently. Because of this the field cannot observe long-term improvements in these embeddings and cannot make fair comparisons between different approaches. The second is that when a practitioner has to decide which phonetic word embedding method to use, the usual approach is to apply the embeddings first, which is generally fast, and then train a downstream model on them, which takes a lot of compute and time. Instead, intrinsic evaluation metrics for embeddings, which are cheap, could give useful signals for choosing an embedding method before training the downstream models, which is expensive, but only if they are shown to correlate well with extrinsic metrics. Unlike for semantic word embeddings, we show that the intrinsic and extrinsic metrics for phonetic word embeddings generally correlate with each other. Prior work has evaluated acoustic word embeddings, but we specialize in phonetic word embeddings for text and not for speech.

Our main contribution is the evaluation suite for phonetic word embeddings, since nothing equivalent exists yet in this subfield. We also contribute multiple methods for phonetic word embeddings and a survey of the existing ones.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Word embeddings are omnipresent in modern NLP [1,2,3]. Their main benefit is that they compress some information into fixed-dimensional vectors. These vectors can be used as machine-learning features for NLP applications, and studying them can reveal linguistic insights [4,5,6]. Word embeddings are often trained with methods from distributional semantics [7] and therefore carry semantic information. For example, the embedding for the word carrot may be more similar to the embeddings for other vegetables than to that of ocean.

Some applications, however, may require a different type of information to be encoded. The orthography, especially in English, can obscure the pronunciation. A poem generation model, for instance, may need embeddings to reflect that ocean rhymes with motion and not with soybean, even though the spelling of the final syllables of the words suggests otherwise (see Figure 1).

Such embeddings, called phonetic word embeddings, contain phonetic information and have been of recent interest [8,9,10,11]. The objective is that words with similar pronunciation are mapped to vectors near each other in the embedding space. Many tasks have benefited from incorporating phonetic word embeddings, including cognate and loanword detection [12,13,14], named entity recognition [15,16], spelling correction [17], and speech recognition [18]. See Section 6.2 for a more detailed list of possible applications.

We introduce four phonetic word embedding methods: count-based, autoencoder, and metric and contrastive learning. While some of these techniques are inspired by previous work, we are the first to apply them with supervision from articulatory feature vectors, a form of linguistic knowledge that is seldom exploited for representation learning.

More importantly, we introduce an evaluation suite for testing the performance of phonetic embeddings. The motivation for this is two-fold. First, prior work evaluates models inconsistently, which prevents the field from observing long-term improvements in such embeddings and from making fair comparisons across approaches. Second, when a practitioner decides which phonetic word embedding method to use, the go-to approach is to first apply the embeddings (generally fast) and then train a downstream model on them (compute and time intensive). Intrinsic embedding evaluation metrics (cheap) could instead provide useful signals for selecting an embedding method before downstream models are trained (expensive), provided they are shown to correlate well with extrinsic metrics. In contrast to semantic word embeddings [19], we show that intrinsic and extrinsic metrics for phonetic word embeddings generally correlate with each other. While [20] evaluate acoustic word embeddings, we specialize in phonetic word embeddings for text rather than speech.

Our main contribution is this evaluation suite for phonetic word embeddings, for which no equivalent yet exists in this subfield. We also contribute multiple methods for phonetic word embeddings and a survey of existing ones.
